accuracy.evidence: Uses the national curriculum wording: Year 4 'describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down', Year 6 'draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane, and reflect them in the axes', and KS3 congruence under rotations, reflections and translations. The lab geometry was checked cell by cell: the slide is exactly 4 right and 2 up, corner A moves 5 right and 3 down, the quarter turn about the bottom corner sends the pole to point right, and copy 2 is a true 180 degree image while copy 3 is the mirror image in a vertical line.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets counting the gap between shape and image instead of the distance one corner travels (mastery m8 and the corner-arrow step), swapping across and up in coordinates ((2, 3) moved 4 right and 1 up wrongly given as (3, 7)), mixing clockwise and anticlockwise (the lab names a wrong-way turn), forgetting the centre of rotation, and calling a mirror image a rotation. The adult notes name each as a common mistake.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagslide is a transformation board: a flag-shaped polyomino is dragged square by square onto a dashed outline, a translation arrow is aimed from a corner to its image, the shape is spun about a centre dot with an animated quarter turn, and three copies are classified. It passes the 30% shingle gate and is unlike flagsymm, which folds shapes on a mirror line, and the coordinates geolab, which plots single points.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step adds one idea with the same flag: a slide keeps size and orientation, one arrow from any corner describes the whole translation, a quarter turn needs a centre and a direction, a half turn ends the same either way, and the facing of a copy tells translation, rotation or reflection apart. The Challenge reuses those ideas with coordinates, combined slides and turn counting.

predictions.evidence: Four of the five build steps ask for a prediction before the child acts: whether a slide changes size, which corner to count from, which way the pole points after a quarter turn clockwise, and whether half turns in opposite directions match. The distractors (gets bigger, only the top corner, points left, end in different places) are the real wrong ideas, and the done message quotes the pick back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions with a tagged reason for every wrong answer in why(): naming a slide as a turn or flip, adding the up move to the wrong number, swapping across and up, miscounting quarter turns, thinking a move changes size, confusing a half turn with a quarter or full turn, and subtracting or multiplying combined translations. A rule card above the questions sums up slide, turn and flip.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and name the formal words translation, rotation and reflection alongside slide, turn and flip, with a clock hand picture for a quarter turn. The adult notes quote the curriculum and explain vectors and the three facts a rotation needs in plain sentences. Each lab step has two or three sentences, and the canvas status line gives the move in words.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries content: the kid text gives the three moves and the same-size rule, and the adult text gives the curriculum link, how each move is described, the named mistakes and what the lab does. The family tip is a card-and-grid game with called-out moves. The content gate found no stock phrases, and similarity to other lessons is under the 12% limit.

mobile.evidence: Checked at the iPhone 13 viewport in light and dark and on desktop: the 12 by 8 board fits the canvas width, the four arrow buttons and the two turn buttons are large and wrap in one row, drags snap to whole squares so a thumb does not need precision, and copies can be chosen by tapping the cells or the Copy buttons. The browser walk drives every step on desktop and phone.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin with an aria-label (slide one square left, up, down or right; move the arrow tip; quarter turn clockwise or anticlockwise; choose copy 1 to 3). say() updates the canvas aria-label and live caption with the move in words, for example 'So far: 4 right, 1 up'. Copies are numbered so colour is never the only cue, and turning respects reduced motion by skipping the animation.
